title: Singing scripture
hookLine: the Guru Granth Sahib is sung in set musical modes

lines: A HEADING THAT GIVES A TUNE.
cards: Turn past the opening prayers of the Guru Granth Sahib, and look at the heading over the next hymn. In a novel, a heading gives you a chapter, or a topic. This one gives you a tune: Sri Raag.
Then it tells you which Guru is speaking. Then the words. Before the meaning, the music.
Page after page, the headings change: Raag Gauri, Raag Asa, Raag Sorath. The scripture is laid out like a songbook, because that's how it's meant to be heard.
Five days ago, kirtan meant a room singing names back and forth. Today, the same word, and a different thing: scripture, sung.

teach.b: In Sikh life, kirtan is the singing of gurbani, the Guru's word: the hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib, sung in the musical modes, the ragas, that the scripture itself names. A raga is more than a scale.
In Indian music, tradition ties each raga to a mood, and often to a time of day or a season. So when the heading names a raga, it's saying how the words should feel when they reach you.

Tradition tells that Guru Nanak traveled with a Muslim musician, Bhai Mardana, who played the rebab, a stringed instrument, while the Guru sang. From the beginning, in the Sikh telling, the word came with music.
In a gurdwara today, singers called ragis sit before the Guru Granth Sahib, often with harmonium and tabla, and sing its hymns.

teach.h: NO NEW WORDS: THE WORDS ARE SCRIPTURE.
teach.b: They don't bring new words; the words are the scripture. What changes is the singing. And the scripture speaks of this itself.

In a hymn of Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, a line says, in paraphrase, that in this dark age, kirtan is foremost. In Sikh teaching, the Guru Granth Sahib is the living Guru. So to sing it is not to perform about the Guru.
It's to let the Guru's own words be heard the way the pages ask. A sentence read once is gone. A sentence sung comes back on its own, in the shower, in traffic, at night.
Sung scripture goes home with you.

how: In gurdwaras, ragis sing hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib in the ragas named in its headings, often with harmonium and tabla, while the congregation sits and listens or sings along.

games.q: you turn past the opening prayers of the Guru Granth Sahib. what does the heading over the next hymn give you first?
o: a summary of the hymn's meaning.
games.why: a tune: Sri Raag. then which Guru is speaking. then the words. before the meaning, the music.

practice: Listen to the sounds around you as if they were music: the hum of a fridge, a car, your own breath. Then bring to mind one line, from any source, that you know because it was sung, and notice how it arrives, tune first, then words.

wordCard.voice: Kirtan. In Sikh life, the singing of the Guru Granth Sahib's own hymns in the ragas its pages name. Scripture, heard as music. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: singing the praise of God; in Sikh life, the singing of gurbani.

carryVoice: Your line: sung scripture. A melody always brings its words along with it. See you tomorrow.
